title: Mark-up and margin
summary: Work out mark-up and margin from cost and price, and learn why they are different numbers.

blocks.text: A buyer says, "We mark up everything by 50%." The finance manager says, "Our margin target is 30%." They are both talking about profit, but they are not talking about the same number.
You will work out both for four shoe lines and check each against a margin target. Costs, prices and targets are fictional.

items: Objective: calculate mark-up and margin from cost and price, and explain the difference.
You pass the mission at 75% or more in the Assessment.

blocks.text: Worked example. A pair costs 500 and sells for 700. Profit is 700 - 500 = 200. Mark-up is 200 / 500 = 0.4, which is 40%. Margin is 200 / 700 = 0.286, which is 28.6%.

The same profit gives two different percentages because they divide by different numbers. The price is bigger than the cost, so margin is always smaller than mark-up (when there is a profit). A 100% mark-up is only a 50% margin.

To set a price from cost and a mark-up, multiply the cost by 1 plus the mark-up. A cost of 400 with a 50% mark-up gives a price of 400 x (1 + 50%) = 600. Do not add 50% of the price: the mark-up is on the cost.
Tip: always say which one you mean. A target margin is a share of the selling price, so it is the right number to compare with a margin target, as you do in column F.
Four questions on mark-up and margin. Type numbers without commas or the % sign.

items: Mark-up = (price - cost) / cost. Margin = (price - cost) / price.
The same profit gives a smaller margin than mark-up, because the price is bigger than the cost.
Price from cost and mark-up = cost x (1 + mark-up).
Keep targets in a cell, such as $G$2, so the check follows when the target changes.
